highlights: Europe seeks dependable gas amid strategic hedging

frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: European buyers depend on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, giving Algiers leverage but exposing it to pricing pressure and infrastructure competition. Gas transition policies could gradually reduce Algeria's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya creates border-security and smuggling risks. External security partnerships in the Sahel complicate Algeria's preference for non-intervention and regional autonomy.

highlights: Oil remains central to fiscal sovereignty
Chinese finance is being cautiously rebalanced

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon exports dominate foreign-exchange earnings and leave state capacity vulnerable to price swings, declining production, and external investment terms. International operators retain significant technical and financial influence over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Lobito Corridor development attracts U.S., European, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African critical minerals. Angola gains infrastructure leverage but faces pressure to balance competing external financiers and regional interests.

highlights: Port-centered growth is strengthening state revenue

frictionVectors.title: NIGERIA TRADE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Benin's economy and port logistics remain closely tied to Nigerian trade flows and regulatory decisions. Border restrictions or informal-trade crackdowns can quickly erode customs revenue and commercial autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL MILITANT SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and armed-group movement from Burkina Faso and Niger threaten northern communities, parks, and transport routes. Benin is expanding security cooperation, but external support could shape operational priorities and procurement choices.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong institutional control over diamonds, but state revenues remain exposed to global demand, synthetic stones, and the bargaining power of major trading partners. The Debswana partnership remains strategically important to fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND POWER CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic water scarcity and reliance on regional electricity markets constrain industrial expansion. Infrastructure dependence on South African-linked networks limits policy flexibility during droughts or regional supply disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SECTOR RECONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state influence over gold production, refining, and marketing while revising relationships with foreign mining companies. This can increase fiscal capture but also risks deterring investment, encouraging informal mining, and triggering disputes.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The government's turn away from French security cooperation and reliance on Russian-linked support has increased strategic autonomy from Paris while creating new dependency risks. Persistent militant attacks continue to constrain access to mines, roads, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo constrain Burundi's security autonomy. Cross-border militant activity and refugee flows increase dependence on regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign partners are central to transport, energy, and mining development. Limited state capacity weakens Burundi's bargaining position over mineral projects and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, digital systems, and maritime security rely heavily on foreign finance and partnerships, including European, Chinese, and U.S.-linked actors. This creates leverage risks despite strong domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Water scarcity, imported fuel dependence, and climate-sensitive tourism limit sovereign control over essential resources. Renewable-energy expansion is progressing but remains dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Energy and Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, mining, rail, and port projects involve substantial foreign commercial and financial influence. The state retains formal ownership but captures uneven value amid opaque contracting and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-linked insecurity in the Far North, diverts resources and weakens territorial control. Instability also raises the operating leverage of external security and humanitarian actors.

frictionVectors.title: Russia-Linked Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection but narrowed strategic autonomy. Mining access and security cooperation remain closely intertwined, reducing transparency over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Territory
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to contest roads, borderlands, and mining zones. Weak state presence prevents Bangui from exercising consistent control over agricultural, timber, and mineral resources.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to public finance and regime stability, leaving Chad vulnerable to price shocks and foreign operator decisions. Export infrastructure and technical capacity give external firms substantial influence over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships and Border Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown or restructuring of longstanding French security ties has increased uncertainty over external protection. Instability in Sudan, Libya, and the Lake Chad basin compounds pressure on Chad's limited security and fiscal resources.

frictionVectors.title: France–Mayotte Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration and maritime-security tensions complicate bilateral relations. The dispute limits diplomatic space but has not produced sustained confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Connectivity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, external assistance, and foreign-funded transport and energy projects. Limited domestic fiscal capacity constrains sovereign control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Bargain Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to competition among Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while contract renegotiations seek greater state value capture. Weak oversight and opaque supply chains continue to limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east, including M23 activity and alleged external support networks, undermines Kinshasa's territorial authority. Regional diplomacy and security deployments have not yet produced durable control over key corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues dominate exports and public finance, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price volatility and foreign-operated production arrangements. Limited diversification reduces bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external financing supports roads, ports, and urban projects but increases long-term repayment and concession risks. The government retains political control while fiscal space remains constrained.

highlights: Abidjan emerges as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening producer oversight and traceability, but foreign traders and global processors still capture much of the value. New sustainability rules create both leverage and compliance pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's expansion attracts Gulf, Chinese, European, and other investors, improving connectivity while creating competition over concessions and logistics standards. State capacity to negotiate terms is stronger than in many neighboring markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Base Concentration
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but constrain strategic autonomy and heighten exposure to Red Sea escalation. Djibouti's leverage depends on maintaining careful balance among rival powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and rail links tied to Ethiopia generate strategic value, yet debt obligations and external operators limit domestic control over logistics assets. Disruptions in Ethiopian trade or the Red Sea would quickly pressure state finances.

highlights: Nile security remains strategic red line

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocations
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose any Ethiopian dam operating framework that could reduce downstream water security. Negotiations remain vulnerable to regional escalation and diplomatic stalemate.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and foreign-currency shortages are increasing reliance on Gulf investment, multilateral lending, and strategic-asset divestment. This supports liquidity while narrowing policy autonomy in key sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output threatens fiscal stability and increases dependence on foreign operators, service companies, and external markets. Diversification remains limited despite official plans.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure projects remain tied to foreign contractors and politically connected financing arrangements. Limited transparency raises risks of debt exposure and weak domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing regional and extra-regional security interests. External pressure over port access and military partnerships remains persistent.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Mining provides hard currency but relies heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export channels. Sanctions exposure and limited transparency constrain sovereign control over long-term resource value.

highlights: Sugar and logistics face diversification pressure

frictionVectors.title: South African dependency
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs revenue, energy access, and transport corridors remain closely tied to South Africa. Any disruption in regional logistics or fiscal transfers would quickly affect domestic stability.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited fiscal space restricts independent investment in energy, water, and logistics infrastructure. Foreign and regional financing is available but can reinforce dependence on external supply chains.

highlights: Debt and port access remain unresolved

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable maritime access continues to generate friction with Somalia and regional actors. Port arrangements could improve trade security but also invite broader geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages and debt obligations limit autonomy over infrastructure and industrial policy. Multilateral support and creditor negotiations are essential but impose constraints on state-led development.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over oil and mining
Rail and port capacity remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Resource nationalism versus foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and timber. International investors remain essential for capital and technology, creating tension over contract terms and control.

frictionVectors.title: Trans-Gabon railway vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The railway and export corridors are critical to manganese and agricultural supply chains but remain vulnerable to aging infrastructure and financing gaps. External lenders and operators retain significant leverage over national logistics.

highlights: Senegal remains the dominant security and economic partner
Port modernization is vital to commercial autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese dependence and border integration
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport links, energy access, food flows, and security cooperation. This supports stability but limits strategic autonomy and exposes Banjul to regional political pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul port and fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Port inefficiency and foreign participation in fisheries constrain domestic revenue and food security. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

highlights: Gold and lithium policy tests domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty and illegal extraction
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pushing local refining, stricter gold controls, and greater state participation while confronting illegal mining and environmental damage. Foreign firms, trading networks, and domestic political interests compete over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: The IMF program and debt restructuring have stabilized external financing but narrow the government's room for subsidies and infrastructure spending. Conditions may intensify public pressure over strategic assets and foreign creditor influence.

highlights: Junta retains tight control over mining negotiations

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore megaproject could transform state revenues, but rail, port, and processing infrastructure is being built through large foreign-led consortia. Guinea's long-term sovereignty will depend on contract enforcement, local content, and transparent revenue management.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concessions and political centralization
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain dominated by foreign operators and provide limited domestic processing. Military rule increases negotiating leverage in the short term but reduces transparency and raises risks of politicized concessions.

highlights: Political fragility limits control over national assets
Ports, fisheries, and narcotics routes attract external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of fisheries and maritime space
frictionVectors.details: Weak monitoring capacity leaves coastal fisheries vulnerable to foreign fleets and opaque licensing arrangements. The resulting loss of revenue and food security undermines practical sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and trafficking networks
frictionVectors.details: Limited port governance and recurring political instability create openings for transnational criminal networks and external commercial actors. International security and development partners remain necessary but possess substantial influence over state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and IMF-linked reforms constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese-financed rail and port projects remain central to debates over strategic assets and long-term revenue control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and energy investment
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in renewable energy, geothermal power, and emerging mineral projects is expanding faster than local value-chain capacity. Regulatory scrutiny is increasing as Kenya seeks investment without surrendering resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on a larger neighbor's financing, demand, and infrastructure decisions. Construction and compensation disputes remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and mining vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export economy remains exposed to foreign-owned textile supply chains and volatile diamond markets. Limited domestic processing reduces Lesotho's ability to capture value from its labor and mineral resources.

highlights: Ports and rail corridors attract competition

frictionVectors.title: Large-scale mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold projects generate fiscal receipts but leave Liberia reliant on foreign operators, imported equipment, and externally controlled logistics. Contract transparency, community compensation, and local processing remain recurring pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are competing for control of port services, mining corridors, and related infrastructure. Monrovia must balance investment needs against the risk that strategic transport assets serve concession interests more than national development.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt fields, export terminals, and revenue flows despite the formal role of the National Oil Corporation. This fragmentation weakens national bargaining power and encourages opaque side arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, the United Arab Emirates, and other external actors retain leverage through security partnerships, arms support, and energy interests. Their involvement limits Libya's ability to consolidate a unified resource and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependency
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented processing chains, leaving Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles and external financing conditions. The state continues to face pressure to improve royalties, local procurement, and environmental enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Power and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak roads increase dependence on foreign-backed mining infrastructure and imported fuel. This limits domestic industrialization and gives concession holders disproportionate influence over regional development.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Mining Expansion
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals, but limited domestic processing capacity leaves the country vulnerable to low-value extraction and weak bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: IMF Reform Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and fiscal reforms are improving macroeconomic discipline while narrowing policy space over subsidies, public investment and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state shares and tax concessions, especially in gold, but lacks the capital and technical capacity to fully replace international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Vacuum
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security forces has increased external influence while persistent insurgency threatens transport corridors, mining zones and state control outside major cities.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export revenues but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, cross-border coordination with Senegal and external LNG infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Logistics
frictionVectors.details: The country is seeking to diversify beyond iron ore, yet rail and port capacity remain concentrated around foreign-linked extractive projects and exposed to commodity-price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty position over the Chagos Archipelago, but implementation of any settlement remains sensitive to the future of strategic military infrastructure and external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on foreign investment, tourism and offshore financial activity, creating regulatory and reputational vulnerabilities despite strong domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating control and investment in Western Sahara, but the territory remains diplomatically contested and exposes ports, fisheries and mineral projects to legal and geopolitical pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese and North American partners are competing for access to Moroccan phosphate, battery materials, renewable energy and port infrastructure, increasing leverage but also external dependence.

highlights: LNG restart ambitions face sovereignty and security tests

frictionVectors.title: LNG corridor and foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The revival of offshore gas projects depends on foreign energy firms, external financing, and security support around Cabo Delgado. Local instability limits Maputo's bargaining power over timelines, revenues, and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insurgency and displacement
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten communities, transport routes, and energy infrastructure. Regional and international military assistance improves containment but deepens reliance on outside security actors.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen race accelerates
Windfall expectations meet tougher local-content demands

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil ownership and revenue control
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have strengthened Namibia's leverage, but production will rely heavily on international majors, foreign capital, and imported technical capacity. The government faces pressure to secure stronger state participation and durable fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Green hydrogen infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen and ammonia projects require external capital, export infrastructure, and long-term offtake agreements. Land, water, electricity, and employment concerns could challenge the legitimacy of projects framed primarily around foreign markets.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic commodities
Western exit leaves infrastructure and market gaps

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while reducing French influence. Renegotiation raises sovereignty claims but also risks investment delays, legal disputes, and weaker export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and border-security vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Oil export infrastructure toward the Gulf of Guinea remains exposed to insecurity, political friction, and dependence on neighboring transit systems. Reduced Western engagement and uncertain regional relations complicate financing, maintenance, and insurance.

highlights: Oil theft and grid weakness erode gains

frictionVectors.title: Refining, crude supply, and regulatory leverage
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining capacity can reduce reliance on imported fuel, but feedstock access, pipeline security, and market regulation remain contested. Large private operators hold increasing influence over pricing and supply-chain decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign infrastructure finance and strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and other external partners remain important for rail, ports, power, and mineral development. Abuja must balance urgent infrastructure needs with debt exposure, procurement transparency, and control of strategic assets.

highlights: State control remains strong, regional trust weakens
Mineral diplomacy collides with eastern Congo war

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral supply chains and DRC tensions
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's trading and logistics position in regional minerals faces intense scrutiny amid allegations that armed-group networks benefit from cross-border flows. International pressure threatens trade access, aid relationships, and Kigali's reputation as a reliable investment hub.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnerships and diplomatic conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda leverages military and security partnerships abroad to gain revenue and diplomatic influence, while donors increasingly link cooperation to conduct in eastern Congo. This creates tension between strategic autonomy and dependence on external financing and market access.

highlights: Maritime security is the strategic priority

frictionVectors.title: Offshore energy and licensing
frictionVectors.details: Unproven offshore petroleum prospects attract foreign operators, but limited state capacity and uncertain commercial finds constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, fisheries, and maritime-security needs leave the islands reliant on outside partners, creating quiet competition among European, Chinese, and Gulf-linked interests.

highlights: Oil and gas revenue is reshaping diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is reviewing petroleum and mining arrangements to increase national benefit, risking friction with international operators and complicating investment confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing access and coastal control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure, especially involving European and Asian fleets, continues to test enforcement capacity and public claims of maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic port competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles' ports and exclusive economic zone carry outsized strategic value, drawing interest from India, China, and Gulf actors while the government seeks to avoid entanglement.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and climate-finance leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-for-nature and climate-finance arrangements improve conservation capacity but can narrow policy space if external conditions become too prescriptive.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore, rutile, and other mineral projects provide revenue and infrastructure but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign pricing, ownership, and environmental pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-backed infrastructure links can improve trade capacity while creating long-term concerns over debt exposure, concessions, and strategic access.

highlights: Sovereignty is tied to external security guarantees
Offshore resources are entering strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Turkey and offshore energy
frictionVectors.details: Turkish security and energy cooperation strengthens Mogadishu's position, but foreign involvement in offshore exploration raises questions over revenue control and federal-state coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia-Somaliland access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Competing claims over maritime access and recognition continue to internationalize Somalia's territorial sovereignty dispute and complicate regional port politics.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and rail constraints
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity, rail and port weaknesses limit South Africa's ability to process and export minerals on sovereign terms. Reform and private-sector participation are advancing, but infrastructure recovery remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Competing mineral partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, the European Union and Gulf investors are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is pursuing diversification while resisting exclusive alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on a fragile pipeline route through Sudan, leaving revenues exposed to war damage, political leverage and opaque commercial arrangements. Production and fiscal stability are highly vulnerable to disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Regional mediators, international donors and security partners retain substantial influence over the peace process and state capacity. Weak institutions limit Juba's control over oil, land and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and armed-finance networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and export channels are central to financing rival armed actors, with external commercial and political networks competing for access. This diverts resource rents away from national institutions and intensifies sovereignty loss.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea corridor contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated maritime infrastructure are strategically important to regional powers and outside security actors. The war has made access, logistics and reconstruction potential tools of external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: LNG project bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking to advance large offshore LNG development while securing stronger domestic benefits, local content and fiscal protections. Negotiations with international energy companies remain sensitive to price, environmental and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades at Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors are attracting competition among Chinese, Gulf, European and regional interests. The government is balancing financing needs against fears of excessive dependence or strategic concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major trade and transshipment asset, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign operators, lenders and shipping networks. This creates exposure to external commercial influence over a critical national gateway.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover risk
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and political instability in Burkina Faso and northern Benin are increasing pressure on Togo's northern frontier. Security spending and foreign partnerships are expanding, potentially narrowing policy autonomy.

highlights: Phosphate sector remains strategic but underperforming

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financial leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial and migration partnerships provide critical support but give external actors influence over Tunisian border policy and fiscal choices.

frictionVectors.title: Gas import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains heavily dependent on imported energy and transit arrangements with Algeria, leaving its power system exposed to regional supply and pricing pressure.

highlights: Oil infrastructure advances through external partnerships

frictionVectors.title: East African Crude Oil Pipeline
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor deepens Chinese and Gulf-linked project exposure while facing environmental, financing, and community-displacement disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert and regional insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil development around Lake Albert is tied to instability in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, complicating security, logistics, and local control of extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Competing copper corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito, TAZARA, and southern African corridors are drawing competing Western, Chinese, and regional investment, creating leverage but also infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and fiscal capture
frictionVectors.details: Government efforts to secure greater value from copper face pressure from multinational operators, debt obligations, power shortages, and volatile commodity prices.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and battery-mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors dominate much of the lithium-processing and mining expansion, while domestic beneficiation rules have not fully ensured local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency, and mining finance
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, currency instability, and limited access to conventional finance push the state toward opaque bilateral deals and reduce transparency over diamonds, gold, and minerals.
